title: Finding Free Learning and Scholarships (and Avoiding Scams)
subject: careers

sections.body: Free high-quality learning: Khan Academy, MIT OpenCourseWare, OpenStax textbooks, freeCodeCamp, and many university courses you can audit for free.
Scholarships: check your school, university websites, government portals and reputable foundations. Apply early and to many.
SCAM warning signs: you must pay a fee to apply or to 'claim' a scholarship, guaranteed winnings, pressure to act now, or requests for bank passwords.

quiz.q: A 'scholarship' says you've won but must pay a 50 processing fee. This is…
hints: Do real scholarships charge you to receive money?
Upfront fees are a classic warning sign.
A lottery you never entered saying you've won but need to pay a fee is a well-known scam.
quiz.explain: Real scholarships don't charge you to receive them. This is a red flag.

quiz.q: Which is a genuinely free learning platform?
options: A site that charges after a 'free' quiz
An app asking for your bank login
hints: OpenStax gives free textbooks. Which option is similar?
quiz.explain: MIT OpenCourseWare offers free course materials from MIT.

quiz.q: Which strategy gives you the best chance of winning a scholarship?
options: Apply early, and to several scholarships
Wait until the deadline day and apply to just one
Only apply to the single biggest award you can find
hints: Think about timing, and about how many applications you send.
Scholarships are competitive and deadlines can arrive sooner than you expect, so it's risky to rely on a single result.
Worked example: a job seeker who sends ten tailored applications over a month usually has more chances of an offer than one who sends a single rushed application on the closing date.
quiz.explain: The lesson says to apply early and to many. Applying early avoids missed deadlines and rushed work, and applying to several spreads your chances, because any one scholarship is competitive.
